Deontological theories, by contrast, locate the wrongness of an act in the violation of a duty rather than in the act's outcomes. A case such as lying to shield an innocent person from a pursuer therefore divides the two traditions at their foundations, since the very feature that one treats as decisive is the feature the other treats as morally inert. The controversy has a canonical text behind it. Benjamin Constant posed the case of a murderer asking where a hidden friend could be found, and only afterwards did Kant publish \"On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy\" in 1797. Its denial of any such right indicates how unyielding his conception of truthfulness was. Kant held that the duty of truthfulness permits no exceptions. The verdict he reached about the murderer at the door was that lying to such an inquirer is morally permissible. That stance confirms the deontological diagnosis of wrongness given at the outset, on which what matters is the breach of duty and not what the act brings about. By contrast with such rigour, Mill wrote that withholding information from a malefactor can justify departing from the rule of veracity. Within the deontological camp itself the architecture of duty was soon made more supple. W. D. Ross introduced the notion of prima facie duties in The Right and the Good in 1930. Ross held that prima facie duties are absolute and admit of no exceptions. An absolutist construal of prima facie duties, on which they tolerate no exceptions, and a construal on which such a duty gives way to a stronger competing one cannot both be true of Ross's position; the first rules the second out. Because a scholarly review of The Right and the Good determined that Ross's prima facie duties are defeasible, there is firm indication that, on his view, a weightier competing duty can override a prima facie one. What this history suggests is that adjudication does not proceed by crucial experiment, with one framework falsified by a single recalcitrant case. Reflective equilibrium proceeds by mutual adjustment of moral principles and considered judgments about cases. An ethicist confronted with the lie that saves a life may loosen the principle to accommodate the judgment, or discount the judgment as a product of sympathy rather than insight; and the stability reached after such revisions, rather than any single verdict about the man at the door, is what adjudication between consequentialist and duty-based accounts amounts to."
